text: PagedAttention made it possible to share KV cache blocks between requests with identical prefixes. Prompt caching is what actually uses that possibility on purpose.

A long system prompt or a set of few-shot examples often appears, token for token, at the start of many different requests. Without special handling, prefill recomputes that entire shared prefix every single time, at full cost. Prompt caching stores it once and reuses it for every later request that starts the same way.

This happens at two layers. Server-side, the serving framework itself hashes incoming prefixes and checks its existing cache blocks for a match — vLLM does this automatically, no configuration needed. At the API level, hosted providers expose it explicitly: a request marks a breakpoint after reusable content, and that prefix gets cached and billed differently on later calls. Same underlying idea, one automatic, one explicit.

The catch is that the match has to be exact, token for token. Change one earlier word, or insert a timestamp near the top of the prompt, and the cache invalidates for everything after it — which is why production prompt design puts stable, shared content first and variable content last.
In practice: vLLM turns this on with one flag, and it's automatic from there. API-level caching instead asks you to mark the breakpoint explicitly, right after the shared system prompt.

In multi-tenant systems, cache sharing has to stay scoped so it never leaks one tenant's content into another's response. Next up, lesson twenty-two: long-context serving, where this chapter's cache problem gets pushed to its most extreme scale.
